impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method claims directed to a genus of antibodies requires the same breadth-of-genus analysis applied to composition claims, particularly after Amgen v. Sanofi.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied rehearing en banc on a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding creates confusion about enablement standards for method claims and sustains overly broad claims contrary to Supreme Court precedent. The decision preserves a potentially more lenient enablement standard for method claims compared to composition claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims benefit from a potentially more permissive enablement standard, allowing broader genus claims to survive challenge and providing stronger exclusionary rights in the pharmaceutical and biotech sectors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors and generic drug manufacturers face greater difficulty invalidating broad method claims on enablement grounds, potentially blocking entry into therapeutic markets even when the patent holder has only enabled a small portion of the claimed genus.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a performance range (MVTR) are indefinite when the specification identifies multiple testing methods that yield materially different results, and the claims do not specify which method to use.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that Cocona's waterproof membrane patent claims were invalid as indefinite because the claims recited an MVTR range measurable by multiple methods (upright and inverted cup methods) that produce significantly different results, and neither the claims nor specification specified which method defined the claimed range. This ruling reinforces that functional performance limitations must provide reasonable certainty about scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in industries relying on performance-based specifications (textiles, materials, manufacturing) gain a stronger basis to challenge vague performance-metric claims, reducing exposure to overbroad patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims defined by measurable performance parameters must ensure their specifications clearly identify the testing methodology, or risk indefiniteness invalidation. Existing patents with ambiguous measurement limitations face heightened vulnerability.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient for the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether a licensee's shift from commercialization to enforcement constitutes cessation of business operations triggering automatic termination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue in its own name without joining A&M. The court also held that shifting business operations to patent enforcement did not constitute ceasing business operations under the license agreement's termination provision.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent licensing entities and exclusive licensees benefit from clarity that an exclusive license conveying substantially all rights constitutes a virtual assignment, enabling enforcement without joining the patent owner. Universities and licensees structuring technology transfer agreements gain useful guidance.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense based on standing and joinder arguments when facing suits from exclusive licensees. Companies defending against patent enforcement entities cannot argue that a shift to enforcement-only operations terminates the underlying license.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment on trade secret damages and remanded for a new trial, instructing the court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating the original jury verdict. The court affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law arising from Ford's development of competing software while licensing Versata's technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from the court's instruction that trial courts must give adequate consideration to multiple damages methodologies and from the reinstatement of a jury's breach of contract award, strengthening the enforceability of software licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal alternatives while licensing third-party software face significant trade secret misappropriation risk. The remand for reconsideration of additional damages models may result in larger liability exposure for Ford and similarly situated defendants.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether certain claims survive Alice step two based on specific technical limitations.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on patent eligibility in a case involving communication system patents. The court vacated eligibility rulings for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents, finding the latter contained sufficiently specific technical limitations. The court also affirmed infringement and damages findings, including the denial of motions to exclude damages expert testimony.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications and standards-related technology gain guidance on how to draft claims that survive § 101 challenges by including specific technical implementations rather than purely functional recitations. The affirmance of damages methodology supports robust royalty calculations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry standards face continued exposure to patent infringement claims where standard-essential patents survive eligibility challenges. The partial vacatur creates uncertainty about which claim formulations will satisfy Alice.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to a communications apparatus with a coupler matching impedance were indefinite, and whether the claims satisfied the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court found that while the claims were not indefinite, the patent did not enable the full scope of the claimed invention. This case demonstrates that surviving an indefiniteness challenge does not guarantee validity when enablement is separately contested.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers retain a strong alternative invalidity defense through enablement challenges even when indefiniteness arguments fail, providing multiple avenues to challenge overly broad patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that courts may affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not reached by the trial court, making it harder to predict outcomes on appeal and increasing the cost of patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the term 'internal diameter' in a patent directed to oil and gas casing float tools, and whether the resulting infringement and validity determinations were correct.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment finding infringement of a patent related to oil and gas casing flotation tools and remanded for further proceedings. The case turned on the proper construction of 'internal diameter' — a dispute with direct implications for infringement analysis of competing downhole tools in the energy sector.
impacts.positiveImplications: Energy service companies defending against patent infringement claims benefit from the Federal Circuit's willingness to scrutinize claim construction of seemingly straightforward mechanical terms, potentially narrowing the scope of asserted claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the oil and gas equipment space face uncertainty when key claim terms are subject to multiple reasonable interpretations, as vacatur and remand prolongs costly litigation.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent case on § 101 eligibility grounds after already determining that venue is improper and dismissing on that basis.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds. AML did not dispute the merits of either ruling but argued the court should not have reached the eligibility question after finding venue improper. The Federal Circuit held the district court acted within its discretion to address both threshold challenges, establishing that an eligibility dismissal can stand alongside a venue dismissal.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases can obtain dismissals on multiple grounds simultaneously, providing issue-preclusive effect on patent eligibility that may prevent the patent holder from simply refiling in a proper venue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities face greater risk that venue challenges will be coupled with eligibility rulings, potentially invalidating claims before the case can be refiled elsewhere, effectively creating a two-for-one dismissal risk.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient reasoning when denying Rule 11 sanctions and § 285 attorneys' fees motions in a case where the asserted patent claims were found invalid under § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of Rule 11 sanctions and § 285 fees, finding the court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved patents on electronic sweepstakes systems where related patent applications had been rejected under § 101 post-Alice, and a related patent had been invalidated on the same grounds before suit was filed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants who prevail in patent cases on § 101 grounds gain a stronger basis for seeking fee-shifting, particularly where the patent holder had prior notice that its claims were likely ineligible. The ruling requires courts to provide reasoned analysis when denying fee motions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face heightened risk of sanctions and fee awards when asserting patents with related applications or patents that have been rejected or invalidated under § 101, even if the specific patent-in-suit has not been directly challenged.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a contract dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's contingent payment provision tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject matter jurisdiction over a dispute about whether T-Mobile owed an additional payment under a settlement agreement conditioned on whether asserted claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination. The court determined the dispute was fundamentally one of contract interpretation under state law, not a patent law question, and transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies structuring patent litigation settlements with contingent payments tied to PTO proceedings gain clarity that disputes over such provisions will be resolved in regional circuits under state contract law, potentially providing more predictable outcomes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties expecting Federal Circuit expertise on patent-related settlement disputes may find themselves in regional circuits less familiar with patent prosecution terminology, creating uncertainty in interpreting settlement terms that reference PTO proceedings.
